To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the colonial Indian cofradía was a social and cultural institution, and that it was the main ethnic marker in the colonial Valley of Lima.
in the colonial period the urban Indians of Lima were more likely than rural Indians to have a sense of belonging to the Spanish culture and to have a stronger sense of ethnicity.

the colonial Indian ethnicities were a product of the Spanish conquest and the subsequent colonial regime; that the ethnicities were a response to the colonial situation; that the ethnic identities were a product of both the Spanish and the Indian peoples; and that the ethnicities varied in strength, with those in urban areas weaker than those in rural areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which ethnicity was constructed, maintained, and transformed by the Indian people themselves in the context of the colonial world.

how the Spanish conquest and colonization, the introduction of new diseases, the establishment of new social and economic institutions, the formation of a new colonial state, and the creation of a new ethnic category, “indio,” contributed to the disappearance of preconquest ethnic identities.
the ways in which the Indian peoples, both in rural and in urban settings, responded to the new ethnic and racial categories that emerged during the colonial period.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Spanish conquest did not eliminate ethnic distinctions among Indians, but it did contribute to their implosion.
the ethnic implosion of the Indian peoples of the Andes was a gradual process, and it varied in time and place.
ethnic differences among the Indians of colonial Latin America varied in time and place, and were more pronounced in the rural than the urban environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ethnic implosion in Peru, which occurred in the colonial period, did not erase the Indian peoples, as many scholars have argued; rather, it produced a new ethnicity, the “indio,” whose existence is a legacy of the colonial period and whose demise is a product of the twentieth-century.
the Spanish conquest did not obliterate all pre-Hispanic ethnic distinctions, but it did result in the implosion and leveling of ethnic differences among the Indian peoples of Peru.
the ethnic implosion was a gradual, uneven, and incomplete process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethnicities were not static but dynamic and that they were shaped by a variety of forces, including colonialism, which in the Andes resulted in the implosions of many ethnicities.
the colonial cofradía was an ethnic institution, a fact not widely recognized in the scholarship.
the colonial cofradía, a voluntary association of Indians, was the most important institution in the urban context that helped to maintain the ethnic identities of its members.
